primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria caused by an acquired PIGA mutation in a hematopoietic stem-cell clone
mechanism: An acquired PIGA mutation impairs glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor synthesis, preventing complement-regulatory proteins such as CD55 and CD59 from attaching normally to blood-cell surfaces. Loss of these regulators permits complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis and contributes to thrombosis.
vignette: A 34-year-old man has fatigue, episodic dark urine, abdominal pain, and an unprovoked hepatic-vein thrombosis. Laboratory studies show anemia, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, elevated indirect bilirubin, and decreased haptoglobin. Direct antiglobulin testing is negative. Flow cytometry shows a population of granulocytes with markedly reduced CD55 and CD59 expression.
lead: Which molecular defect most directly explains these findings?
correct: An acquired defect in glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchor synthesis caused by a PIGA mutation
distractors: A germline spectrin mutation causing loss of erythrocyte membrane surface area
An acquired JAK2 mutation causing constitutive erythropoietin-receptor signaling
A germline mutation in factor V that prevents its inactivation by activated protein C
Autoantibody-mediated destruction of platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa
distractor_notes: Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis, which is a membrane-cytoskeleton disorder and does not produce loss of CD55/CD59 from multiple blood-cell lineages.
JAK2 mutations are associated with myeloproliferative neoplasms and do not cause GPI-anchor deficiency or complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.
Factor V Leiden increases venous-thrombosis risk but does not explain Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis or reduced CD55/CD59.
Antibodies against platelet glycoproteins cause immune thrombocytopenia rather than a clonal GPI-anchor deficiency affecting complement regulation.
key_expl: PNH is caused by an acquired PIGA mutation in a hematopoietic stem-cell clone. The resulting GPI-anchor deficiency prevents normal surface expression of complement regulators such as CD55 and CD59, producing complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis and a strong thrombotic tendency.
objective: Connect Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis, unusual-site thrombosis, and loss of CD55/CD59 to an acquired PIGA mutation that impairs GPI-anchor synthesis.

outline: Sarcomere mutations and dynamic left-ventricular outflow obstruction
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to an autosomal-dominant sarcomere-protein mutation
mechanism: Pathogenic variants in sarcomere proteins such as beta-myosin heavy chain or myosin-binding protein C cause myocyte hypertrophy and disarray. Asymmetric septal hypertrophy can create dynamic left-ventricular outflow obstruction, which worsens when ventricular volume falls and the septum and mitral valve are brought closer together.
vignette: A 19-year-old collegiate basketball player has exertional presyncope. His father died suddenly at age 36. Examination reveals a harsh systolic murmur along the left sternal border that becomes louder during the Valsalva maneuver. Echocardiography shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.
lead: Which inherited abnormality most likely underlies this patient's disease?
correct: An autosomal-dominant mutation in a cardiac sarcomere protein
distractors: An X-linked mutation causing absence of dystrophin in skeletal and cardiac muscle
A mitochondrial DNA mutation causing impaired oxidative phosphorylation in all tissues
An autosomal-recessive mutation causing defective LDL-receptor internalization
A germline mutation causing constitutive activation of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase
distractor_notes: Dystrophin deficiency causes Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy and can cause dilated cardiomyopathy rather than the classic hypertrophic obstructive phenotype.
Mitochondrial disorders can affect myocardium but do not classically produce this autosomal-dominant family pattern with asymmetric septal hypertrophy and dynamic obstruction.

Autosomal-recessive LDL-receptor adaptor defects can impair receptor internalization and cause severe hypercholesterolemia, but they do not produce asymmetric septal hypertrophy or dynamic left-ventricular outflow obstruction.
RET activation causes MEN2 syndromes and medullary thyroid carcinoma/pheochromocytoma, not familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
key_expl: Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is typically an autosomal-dominant disease of cardiac sarcomere proteins. Common pathogenic variants involve MYH7 or MYBPC3 and produce myocyte hypertrophy/disarray with dynamic outflow obstruction.
objective: Recognize familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and connect its dynamic obstructive physiology to autosomal-dominant sarcomere-protein mutations.

outline: ATP7B-mediated biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin loading
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Wilson disease due to biallelic ATP7B dysfunction
mechanism: ATP7B is a hepatocellular copper-transporting ATPase involved in incorporating copper into ceruloplasmin and exporting excess copper into bile. Loss of ATP7B function impairs both processes, causing hepatic copper accumulation and reduced circulating ceruloplasmin.
vignette: A 17-year-old boy has tremor, dysarthria, behavioral changes, and elevated aminotransferases. Slit-lamp examination shows brownish rings at the corneal periphery. Serum ceruloplasmin is low, and 24-hour urinary copper excretion is increased.
lead: Which cellular function is most directly impaired in this disorder?
correct: Hepatocellular transport of copper into bile and incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin
distractors: Intestinal export of absorbed copper into portal blood by ATP7A
Lysosomal degradation of sphingomyelin within macrophages
Conversion of ferric iron to ferrous iron at the duodenal brush border
Hepatic conjugation of bilirubin with glucuronic acid
distractor_notes: ATP7A participates in intestinal copper handling and is defective in Menkes disease; Wilson disease is caused by ATP7B dysfunction in hepatocytes.
Sphingomyelin degradation is impaired in Niemann-Pick disease and is unrelated to copper transport.
Duodenal iron reduction is part of iron absorption and does not explain hepatic copper accumulation, low ceruloplasmin, or Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Bilirubin conjugation defects cause disorders such as Gilbert or Crigler-Najjar syndrome and do not produce the copper phenotype described.
key_expl: Wilson disease results from ATP7B dysfunction. ATP7B normally helps load copper onto ceruloplasmin and moves excess copper from hepatocytes into bile. Failure of these processes causes copper accumulation in liver and other tissues.
objective: Connect Wilson disease to ATP7B dysfunction that impairs biliary copper excretion and copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin.

outline: Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism and impaired ammonium excretion
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Type 4 renal tubular acidosis due to hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism
mechanism: Reduced renin and aldosterone impair distal potassium and hydrogen handling, causing hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia suppresses proximal-tubular ammoniagenesis, reducing urinary ammonium buffering and net acid excretion and producing a hyperchloremic normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
vignette: A 68-year-old man with long-standing diabetes mellitus and mild chronic kidney disease has persistent serum potassium of 5.8 mEq/L. Serum bicarbonate is 18 mEq/L and chloride is elevated; the anion gap is normal. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone concentration are both low.
lead: Which renal process most directly contributes to this patient's metabolic acidosis?
correct: Reduced ammonium excretion due to hyperkalemia-associated suppression of renal ammoniagenesis
distractors: Increased proximal bicarbonate wasting caused by defective carbonic anhydrase activity
Failure of alpha-intercalated cells to lower urinary pH below 5.5 despite normal aldosterone
Excessive ammonium generation in the proximal tubule with increased net acid excretion
Increased distal sodium delivery causing excessive hydrogen and potassium secretion
distractor_notes: Proximal bicarbonate wasting describes type 2 RTA, not the hyperkalemic hypoaldosteronism pattern.
A primary distal-acidification defect describes type 1 RTA; type 4 RTA can still acidify urine because the central problem is insufficient ammonium availability and aldosterone effect.
Type 4 RTA is characterized by reduced, not increased, ammonium excretion.
Increased distal sodium delivery promotes potassium and hydrogen secretion and would oppose the hyperkalemic acidosis.
key_expl: In type 4 RTA, hypoaldosteronism produces hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia suppresses proximal ammoniagenesis, so less NH3 is available to trap secreted hydrogen as NH4+, reducing net acid excretion and causing a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
objective: Explain the metabolic acidosis of type 4 RTA by linking hypoaldosteronism-induced hyperkalemia to reduced renal ammoniagenesis and ammonium excretion.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
Hemicord lesion and tract crossing patterns
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Right-sided Brown-Sequard syndrome from spinal cord hemisection
mechanism: The lateral corticospinal tract has already crossed in the caudal medulla, so a spinal hemicord lesion causes ipsilateral weakness below the lesion. Dorsal-column fibers ascend ipsilaterally in the cord and cross in the medulla, so vibration/proprioception loss is also ipsilateral. Spinothalamic fibers cross within the spinal cord shortly after entry, so unilateral cord injury causes contralateral pain-temperature loss beginning slightly below the lesion.
vignette: A 29-year-old man is stabbed in the right side of the back at the T8 level. Below the injury he has right-leg weakness and loss of vibration and position sense on the right. Pain and temperature sensation are decreased on the left beginning a few segments below the lesion.
lead: Which pattern of tract injury best explains these findings?
correct: Right corticospinal and dorsal-column injury with right-sided spinothalamic tract interruption after crossed pain-temperature fibers enter that tract
distractors: Left corticospinal and dorsal-column injury with left spinothalamic tract interruption
Bilateral dorsal-column injury with sparing of corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts
Central-cord injury affecting only crossing spinothalamic fibers at the anterior white commissure
Right dorsal-root injury causing ipsilateral loss of all sensory modalities without motor deficits
distractor_notes: The weakness and proprioceptive loss are ipsilateral to the right-sided hemicord lesion, not left-sided.
Bilateral posterior-column disease would not explain ipsilateral weakness plus contralateral pain-temperature loss.
A central-cord lesion such as syringomyelia preferentially affects crossing spinothalamic fibers and does not produce the classic hemicord triad.
A dorsal-root lesion is sensory only and would not cause ipsilateral corticospinal weakness or contralateral spinothalamic sensory loss.
key_expl: Brown-Sequard syndrome causes ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration/proprioception below the lesion, plus contralateral loss of pain and temperature because spinothalamic fibers cross in the spinal cord before ascending.
objective: Use spinal-tract crossing anatomy to explain the characteristic ipsilateral motor/proprioceptive and contralateral pain-temperature deficits of Brown-Sequard syndrome.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Pemphigus vulgaris due to IgG autoantibodies against desmogleins
mechanism: IgG autoantibodies target desmoglein adhesion molecules within desmosomes, disrupting keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion. The resulting acantholysis produces fragile intraepidermal blisters, mucosal erosions, and a positive Nikolsky sign.
vignette: A 54-year-old woman develops painful oral erosions followed by flaccid skin blisters that rupture easily. Gentle lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin causes the epidermis to shear away. Biopsy shows suprabasal acantholysis.
lead: Autoantibodies against which cellular structure most directly cause this disorder?
correct: Desmoglein-containing desmosomes that mediate keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion
distractors: Hemidesmosomes that anchor basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane
Type VII collagen anchoring fibrils beneath the basement membrane
Desmin intermediate filaments within skeletal muscle fibers
Integrins on neutrophils that bind endothelial adhesion molecules
distractor_notes: Hemidesmosomal antigens are targeted in bullous pemphigoid, which produces tense subepidermal blisters and usually spares mucosa.
Type VII collagen is targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, a subepidermal blistering disorder.
Desmin is a muscle intermediate filament and is not responsible for epidermal cell-cell adhesion.
Leukocyte integrins participate in immune-cell trafficking rather than keratinocyte adhesion.
key_expl: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by IgG autoantibodies against desmogleins, cadherin-family proteins in desmosomes. Loss of desmosomal adhesion causes acantholysis and fragile intraepidermal blisters.
objective: Connect flaccid bullae, mucosal erosions, positive Nikolsky sign, and suprabasal acantholysis to IgG-mediated disruption of desmoglein-containing desmosomes.

outline: LYST-dependent lysosomal trafficking and giant granules
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Chediak-Higashi syndrome caused by biallelic LYST mutations
mechanism: LYST regulates lysosomal and lysosome-related organelle trafficking, size, and fission. Loss of function produces enlarged fused lysosomal granules in leukocytes and other cells, impairing neutrophil antimicrobial function and cytotoxic-cell degranulation while also disrupting melanosomes and platelet dense granules.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent pyogenic skin and respiratory infections, easy bruising, and partial oculocutaneous albinism. Peripheral blood smear shows neutrophils containing very large azurophilic cytoplasmic granules.
lead: Which cellular defect most directly explains this patient's findings?
correct: Impaired lysosomal trafficking due to loss of LYST function, producing giant dysfunctional granules
distractors: Failure of NADPH oxidase to generate a respiratory burst in phagocytes
Defective integrin expression preventing firm leukocyte adhesion to endothelium
Failure of lysosomal enzymes to receive mannose-6-phosphate targeting signals
Defective platelet dense-body formation caused by an AP3B1 trafficking mutation
distractor_notes: NADPH oxidase deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease with catalase-positive infections but does not cause partial albinism and pathognomonic giant leukocyte granules.
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency causes impaired extravasation, delayed cord separation, and absent pus; it does not cause giant granules or pigment dilution.

I-cell disease is caused by defective mannose-6-phosphate tagging and produces lysosomal enzyme misdirection with coarse features and skeletal abnormalities, not this immunodeficiency-albinism pattern.

AP3B1 mutations can cause Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome type 2 with albinism and immune abnormalities, but the classic pathognomonic giant leukocyte granules identify Chediak-Higashi syndrome due to LYST.
key_expl: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by biallelic LYST mutations that disrupt lysosomal trafficking and organelle fission. The resulting giant fused granules impair leukocyte function and also affect melanosomes and platelet dense granules, explaining recurrent infections, partial albinism, and bleeding tendency.
objective: Recognize Chediak-Higashi syndrome from recurrent pyogenic infections, partial albinism, bleeding tendency, and giant leukocyte granules and connect it to defective LYST-mediated lysosomal trafficking.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency due to SRD5A2 mutation
mechanism: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone. DHT is particularly important for masculinization of the external genitalia during embryogenesis. Deficiency causes undervirilized external genitalia in a 46,XY individual despite preserved anti-Müllerian hormone activity; rising testosterone at puberty can produce partial virilization.
vignette: A 13-year-old child raised as a girl is evaluated for increasing muscle mass, deepening of the voice, and phallic enlargement at puberty. Karyotype is 46,XY. Testes are present in the inguinal canals, and imaging shows no uterus. Serum testosterone is normal for a pubertal male, but dihydrotestosterone is markedly decreased.
lead: Which enzymatic reaction is impaired in this patient?
distractors: Conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone
Conversion of androstenedione to testosterone
Conversion of testosterone to estradiol
Conversion of 17-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol
distractor_notes: Failure of cholesterol side-chain cleavage would broadly impair steroidogenesis and would not produce normal pubertal testosterone with selectively low DHT.
Impaired 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity lowers testosterone production rather than producing a normal testosterone level with low DHT.
Aromatase converts testosterone to estradiol; its deficiency has a different phenotype and does not explain undervirilized external genitalia from low DHT.
21-hydroxylase catalyzes this cortisol-pathway step; its deficiency causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia rather than selective DHT deficiency.
key_expl: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 converts testosterone to DHT. DHT is required for normal masculinization of the external genitalia; affected 46,XY individuals may have undervirilized genitalia at birth and increased virilization at puberty when testosterone rises.
objective: Recognize 5-alpha-reductase deficiency and identify the impaired conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone as the biochemical defect.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Acrodermatitis enteropathica due to an SLC39A4 zinc-transporter defect
mechanism: SLC39A4 encodes the ZIP4 zinc uptake transporter in the small intestine. Autosomal-recessive loss of function impairs enteral zinc absorption, producing zinc deficiency with periorificial/acral dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea, impaired wound healing, and immune dysfunction.
vignette: An 11-month-old boy develops chronic diarrhea, patchy alopecia, and sharply demarcated erythematous plaques around the mouth and on the hands and feet several weeks after weaning. Growth has slowed.
lead: Which inherited defect most likely explains this child's condition?
correct: Loss of function of the intestinal ZIP4 zinc transporter encoded by SLC39A4
distractors: Loss of function of the intestinal apical iron transporter DMT1
Failure to synthesize transcobalamin II for vitamin B12 transport
Loss of pancreatic lipase causing isolated triglyceride malabsorption
Defective renal reabsorption of neutral amino acids due to a proximal-tubule transporter mutation
distractor_notes: DMT1 dysfunction primarily impairs iron uptake and would produce an iron-handling disorder rather than the classic zinc-deficiency triad.
Transcobalamin II deficiency causes cellular vitamin B12 deficiency with hematologic and neurologic consequences, not the periorificial/acral dermatitis-diarrhea-alopecia pattern.
Pancreatic lipase deficiency causes fat malabsorption and steatorrhea but does not specifically produce inherited zinc deficiency from impaired intestinal zinc uptake.
Neutral-amino-acid transport defects can cause Hartnup disease with pellagra-like photosensitive dermatitis, which differs from the periorificial/acral zinc-deficiency phenotype.
key_expl: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal-recessive zinc-absorption disorder caused by pathogenic variants in SLC39A4, which encodes the intestinal ZIP4 zinc transporter. The classic phenotype includes periorificial/acral dermatitis, diarrhea, and alopecia.
objective: Recognize acrodermatitis enteropathica after weaning and connect the phenotype to loss of the SLC39A4-encoded intestinal ZIP4 zinc transporter.

outline: Acetylcholinesterase phosphorylation, aging, and pralidoxime timing
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Organophosphates phosphorylate and inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing acetylcholine accumulation at muscarinic, nicotinic, and central synapses. With time, the phosphorylated enzyme undergoes aging, strengthening the bond so oxime reactivation is no longer effective; pralidoxime is therefore most useful before aging occurs.
vignette: A farm worker is brought to the emergency department after pesticide exposure. He has miosis, diaphoresis, copious bronchial secretions, vomiting, bradycardia, and diffuse muscle fasciculations. Atropine is administered. Pralidoxime is also given promptly because its ability to restore enzyme activity decreases with time.
lead: Which molecular change best explains the time-dependent loss of pralidoxime effectiveness?
correct: Aging of phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase, making the organophosphate-enzyme bond resistant to oxime reactivation
distractors: Competitive displacement of acetylcholine from muscarinic receptors by the organophosphate
Irreversible internalization of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors from the neuromuscular junction
Depletion of presynaptic acetylcholine vesicles after prolonged cholinergic stimulation
Covalent inhibition of choline acetyltransferase, preventing new acetylcholine synthesis
distractor_notes: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase rather than competitively blocking muscarinic receptors; atropine is the muscarinic receptor antagonist.
The primary toxic lesion is acetylcholinesterase inhibition, not irreversible nicotinic-receptor internalization.
The toxidrome results from excess acetylcholine because degradation is impaired, not depletion of acetylcholine stores.
Organophosphates do not exert their main effect by inhibiting choline acetyltransferase.
key_expl: Pralidoxime can reactivate phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase if given before the inhibited enzyme undergoes aging. After aging, the organophosphate-enzyme bond becomes effectively irreversible and new enzyme synthesis is required.
objective: Explain why pralidoxime must be given early in organophosphate poisoning by linking treatment efficacy to aging of phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase.
